AvRate, part two: what does a wicket cost?

We have covered AvRate for batters earlier. This time we turn the scoreboard round. For a bowler, AvRate asks a simpler question: what did each wicket cost you, in runs and in time?

IJ
Ivan Joseph The Grass Bank™ Opinion
November 19, 2026

The other end of the pitch

Cranky and Banky were never going to leave it at the batters. A batter's job is to stay. A bowler's job is to end that stay, and every wicket comes with a price.

Cranky, naturally, looks at the runs. Bowling average is runs conceded per wicket, and he will tell you that a bowler who gives away 21 runs for every scalp is worth his weight in gold. He is right.

Banky looks at the clock. Strike rate is balls bowled per wicket, and he will tell you that a wicket in the 40th ball of a spell wins Tests, while a wicket in the 70th often just tidies up a draw. He is also right.

They are describing the same wicket. One is counting what it cost in runs, the other what it cost in deliveries which in effect is time. AvRate simply adds the two together.

Two prices for one wicket

Average tells you how expensive a bowler was. It rewards accuracy, discipline and the refusal to give anything away. Glenn McGrath built a career on it: 563 wickets at 21.64.

But average is blind to time, exactly as it was for batters. A Test has five days, and you need twenty wickets in them. A bowler who goes for very little but takes 70 balls per wicket can bowl you into a stalemate. The runs dried up; the wickets didn't come.

Strike rate fixes that and breaks something else. A bowler who takes a wicket every 40 balls is a match-winner, unless each one costs 35 runs. Then he is buying wickets on credit, and the opposition is happy to sell.

So we do what we did for the batters:

{AvRate} = {Bowling average} + {Strike rate}

One change from part one: for bowlers, lower is better. A low average means cheap wickets. A low strike rate means quick ones. A low AvRate means both, and that is the bowler you want with the new ball on day one and the old one on day five.

As a rule of thumb, anything under 70 is extraordinary, under 80 is great, and over 100 means the wickets came slowly, expensively, or both.

So who are the best ever by this metric?

To keep out the brilliant but brief, I have used a bar of 200+ Test wickets. That leaves 87 bowlers in the history of the game. Here are the top 20:

Kagiso Rabada is the best wicket-taker Test cricket has produced by this measure, and he is still playing. A wicket every 40 balls, across 350 of them, is the lowest strike rate in the list by almost three balls. Like Harry Brook in part one, the verdict waits for retirement, but for now the number is hard to argue with.

Jasprit Bumrah is second, and his are the cheapest wickets in the top 20: under 20 runs apiece. He too is still playing so the verdict waits for retirement. Dale Steyn completes a podium that would frighten any top order in any era.

Then look at Glenn McGrath, at 15. On average alone he is sixth on this list, and Cranky would put him higher still. But Steyn took his wickets nearly ten balls sooner. McGrath strangled batters; Steyn removed them. Both win Tests, but one does it on a shorter clock.

Curtly Ambrose tells the same story from further down. Only Bumrah, Marshall and Garner bowled cheaper, yet Ambrose is 20th. Batters rarely scored off him, and they often didn't need to. They just had to survive.

Nineteen of the twenty are fast bowlers. The lone spinner is Ravichandran Ashwin at 17, which says as much about the metric as about the men. We will come back to that.

And the batting list had seven Australians in its top 20. The bowling list has five, which goes a long way towards explain why they are the team with the most wins in history.

Country by country

Same bar as above, 200+ wickets, except Sri Lanka and Bangladesh , where I have dropped it to 150 to get five names. Was able to with SL but not with Bangla who still have only three.

England's top five:

Fiery Fred is still England's best, sixty years on. Truly a remarkable bowler! Bow Willis as second best ever may surprise some since he played with Botham and it was Botham who stole the limelight but these numbers tell the right story. Darren Gough at third will also surprise some, but he took his wickets quicker than both Anderson and Broad! And the two of them, who shared a new ball for fifteen years, are separated by 0.14. This is our Lara and Tendulkar moment: Anderson is cheaper, Broad is quicker, and the sum remarkably is a dead heat. Cranky and Banky can both claim victory but this one can be a raging coffee table debate with he said she said replaced by he saw, she saw to tie break.

Australia's top five:

Pat Cummins leads, and Mitchell Starc, often criticised for leaking runs, is second, because no Australian with 200 wickets has taken them faster. Starc is the purest Banky bowler in this piece: the most expensive average in the Australian five, the quickest strike rate. Shane Warne, at 82.91, does not make it. The spinners' problem again.

India's top five:

For a country that produced its bowling greats in spin, this list is a revolution. Bumrah is twelve points clear of anyone India has ever had. Ashwin is the best spinner in the whole list of 87, and Shami sneaks in ahead of Jadeja. Kapil Dev (93.57), Anil Kumble (95.64) and Zaheer Khan (93.37) miss out, and Kumble fans will have plenty to say about that. The case for him rests on 619 wickets and a lot of overs, which AvRate does not reward. Using AvRate we've been able to separate BS Chandrasekhar, the architect of that Oval victory with 6-38 in the second innings as the best among Bedi, Prasanna, Venkatraghavan and himself. Clarity that was absent before.

South Africa's top five:

The strongest five of any country. Four of them are in the all-time top 13, and the averages run from 22.11 to 23.12, almost a straight line. What separates them is pace of wicket-taking, and that is exactly what AvRate measures. Shaun Pollock was as miserly as any of them, but he took his wickets fifteen to eighteen balls later than Steyn or Rabada.

West Indies' top five:

No surprise at the top. Malcolm Marshall was the most complete fast bowler of the great West Indian era, and the numbers agree. Courtney Walsh, with 519 wickets, is just outside at 82.29. The averages of Marshall, Garner and Ambrose are within four hundredths of a run of each other. If you ever needed proof that the West Indies attack was a single machine, there it is.

Pakistan's top five:

Here is the coffee-shop debate. Wasim and Waqar averaged almost exactly the same, 23.62 and 23.56. But Waqar's toe-crushers came eleven balls sooner, and that puts him more than eleven points clear. Many people would still pick Wasim. Imran is right in the middle of these two and what a bowler he was! AvRate says the yorker was the quicker way to a wicket. Shoaib Akhtar (178 wickets, 71.44 AvRate) falls just short of the 200 bar, or he would be second.

New Zealand's top five:

Sir Richard stands nearly ten points clear of anyone New Zealand has produced since. Neil Wagner ahead of Trent Boult will raise eyebrows, but the bouncer barrage worked, and it worked quickly. Shane Bond? Well more on him at the end.

Sri Lanka's top five (150+ wickets):

The gap between Murali and everyone else is the story of Sri Lankan cricket for twenty years. Eight hundred wickets, at a price most fast bowlers never matched, and he is the second-best spinner in the 87.

Bangladesh's top three (150+ wickets):

Perhaps too early for Bangladesh given their short history. All three in the list have averages and SRs that have some way to go before they can be considered among the elite bowlers. But with their recent track record including an impressive win away against Australia, spearheaded by their bowlers, including some quicks they are trending in the right direction.

The spinners' problem

Only one spinner made the top 20, and only two made the top 30. That isn't because spinners are worse. It is because they do a different job.

A spinner bowls long spells, often into the wind, often to hold an end while the quicks rest. He gets fewer new balls, fewer green tops and fewer tired tail-enders. His strike rate will almost always be higher, and AvRate punishes that. So spinners are best compared with each other:

Ashwin over Murali over Warne. Expect that one to run and run. Was he in fact the greatest of them all? What do you think? Let's debate this in our own coffee shop aka comments section.

Stuart MacGill, who spent a career in Warne's shadow, finishes level with him, which tells you how good he was. In fact whenever they played together, he had the better numbers which is a quiz question that might trip most people up.


Does it survive the statisticians?

In part one, the defence was that average and strike rate are both measured in runs. For bowlers that's not true: average is runs per wicket, strike rate is balls per wicket.

But look at what they share. Both are a price per wicket. One is paid in runs, the other in deliveries, which is to say in time. A wicket that costs 22 runs and 45 balls is a cheaper wicket than one that costs 22 runs and 60 balls, and AvRate says so.

Strike rates vary much more than averages: across our 87 bowlers, from about 40 to 88 balls a wicket, against 20 to 34 runs. So in practice AvRate rewards quick wickets more than cheap ones. That is deliberate. You need twenty wickets in five days, and a cheap wicket that takes all session can still cost you the match. As with the batters, lower on either side always means a better AvRate.

The fine print

The Bond problem. Shane Bond took 87 Test wickets at 22.09, one every 38.8 balls. His AvRate of 60.85 would put him above Rabada. Marco Jansen, 102 wickets in, sits at 60.09. Both were or are terrific bowlers, but a short career is not a career's worth of evidence. That is why the bar is 200 wickets.

The Barnes problem. Unlike balls faced in the early batting records, balls bowled were counted from the start, so the old numbers are real. They are also from a different game. SF Barnes took 189 wickets at 16.43 on uncovered pitches before the First World War, an AvRate of 58.09. George Lohmann's 112 wickets at 10.76 come to 53.63. Neither is in our table because neither reached 200, but they are a reminder that the further back you go, the less like-for-like the comparison is.

The era problem. In fast-scoring eras, averages go up and strike rates come down, because batters take more risks. The two halves of AvRate partly cancel out. Partly is not entirely, so a modern bowler and a 1950s bowler with the same AvRate did not necessarily do the same job.

The workload problem. AvRate measures quality per wicket, not quantity. James Anderson took 704 wickets and bowled for 21 years; Rabada has half as many so far. Murali took 800. Durability is a separate virtue, and AvRate doesn't try to measure it.

The last word

For a batter, AvRate asks whether he stayed and whether the stay mattered. For a bowler, it asks what each wicket cost: in runs, and in time. The great ones were cheap on both counts, and they kept it up for a whole career.

Banky gets the last word: "Quick wickets win Tests. Now we can prove it."

Cranky gets the last grumble: "Cheap wickets win them too. McGrath would have told you that, slowly."
